# CM.com Documentation

Guides, API references, and tutorials for CM.com's products.

> Each product below links to its own llms.txt, which contains a full index of that product's documentation pages.
>
> For the complete documentation archive in a single file, use the [Full Documentation Archive](https://docs.cm.com/llms-full.txt).

## When to use this documentation

- Integrating or calling a CM.com API: messaging (SMS, WhatsApp, RCS, email), payments, voice, verification, electronic signing, ticketing.
- Finding an endpoint, request body, error code or webhook of a CM.com product, or generating a client from its OpenAPI specification.
- Not for account actions, billing or live status: this site is documentation only and cannot send a message or take a payment.

## Products

- [Conversational AI](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/llms.txt): Build AI-powered chatbots, automate conversations, and add web chat to your website.
- [Conversational Router](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/llms.txt): Router brings your conversations to the right destination—intelligently connecting all your chat applications into one seamless, unified platform.
- [Customer Engagement](https://docs.cm.com/customer-engagement/llms.txt): Manage customer service inboxes, run marketing campaigns, track behavior, and automate outreach.
- [Email Gateway API](https://docs.cm.com/email-gateway-api/llms.txt): Send transactional and marketing emails with delivery tracking, scheduling, and webhook support.
- [Governance](https://docs.cm.com/governance/llms.txt): Centralized access management platform controlling who can access what resources under which conditions.
- [Halo](https://docs.cm.com/halo/llms.txt): Halo AI platform APIs for core operations and analytics.
- [Live Entertainment](https://docs.cm.com/live/llms.txt): Build ticket shops, manage events and venues, handle reservations, and scan barcodes.
- [Marketplace](https://docs.cm.com/marketplace/llms.txt): Integrate external platforms once, then automatically cascade data contracts, authentication, and authorization across CM products.
- [Messaging](https://docs.cm.com/messaging/llms.txt): Send and receive messages across SMS, WhatsApp, RCS, Apple Messages, Viber, and more from a single API.
- [Mobile Marketing Cloud](https://docs.cm.com/mobile-marketing-cloud/llms.txt): Reach customers with campaigns and email, validate addresses, and build on the Customer Data Platform, Webtracker and product feed.
- [Mobile Service Cloud](https://docs.cm.com/mobile-service-cloud/llms.txt): Customer service software — Agent Inbox, Widget API, Scripted Chatbot and Conversational Router.
- [Payments](https://docs.cm.com/payments/llms.txt): Accept online payments via iDEAL, credit cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Bancontact, and more.
- [Sign](https://docs.cm.com/sign/llms.txt): Send PDF documents to one or more recipients for electronic signing. Signed documents are certified with a trusted digital certificate.
- [Verification](https://docs.cm.com/verification/llms.txt): Verify users with OTP, Number Verify, ID Scan, IBAN checks, and iDIN — all from one platform.
- [Voice](https://docs.cm.com/voice/llms.txt): Request and port phone numbers, build call flows, send calls through the Voice API, and manage SIP accounts, audio, and call insights.

## For AI agents

- [API catalog](https://docs.cm.com/.well-known/api-catalog): every CM.com OpenAPI specification (RFC 9727 linkset)
- [MCP server](https://docs.cm.com/mcp): search and read this documentation and the OpenAPI specifications (Streamable HTTP)

## AI System Prompts

Use these prompt.txt files to give AI coding assistants specialized knowledge of each CM.com product:

- [Conversational AI prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/prompt.txt)
- [Conversational Router prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/prompt.txt)
- [Customer Engagement prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/customer-engagement/prompt.txt)
- [Email Gateway API prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/email-gateway-api/prompt.txt)
- [Governance prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/governance/prompt.txt)
- [Halo prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/halo/prompt.txt)
- [Live Entertainment prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/live/prompt.txt)
- [Marketplace prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/marketplace/prompt.txt)
- [Messaging prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/messaging/prompt.txt)
- [Mobile Marketing Cloud prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/mobile-marketing-cloud/prompt.txt)
- [Mobile Service Cloud prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/mobile-service-cloud/prompt.txt)

- [Sign prompt.txt](https://docs.cm.com/sign/prompt.txt)

# CM.com Documentation > CM.com provides APIs for messaging, payments, voice, verification, electronic signing, ticketing, and more. --- # Conversational AI > Build AI-powered chatbots, automate conversations, and add web chat to your website. --- ## Connect Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/connect.md Integrate Conversational AI with your existing systems. Connect enables data exchange between your bot and external services via **webhooks**. ## How it works When a conversation reaches a point where external data is needed (e.g., checking order status), the bot sends a webhook request to your server. Your server responds with the data, and the bot continues the conversation. ## Key capabilities | Integration type | Description | | - | - | | **Transaction Script Webhook** | Execute custom logic during conversations (e.g., create a booking, update a record) | | **Context Variable Webhook** | Fetch external data to enrich the conversation (e.g., look up a customer profile) | | **Custom integrations** | Build tailored connections to any REST API | ## Example: Transaction webhook Your bot asks a user for their order number, then calls your API to look up the order: ```json { "webhook_url": "https://yourapi.com/orders", "method": "POST", "body": { "order_id": "{{context.order_number}}" } } ``` Your server returns the order details, and the bot uses them in its response: ```json { "status": "shipped", "tracking_number": "1Z999AA10123456784", "estimated_delivery": "2026-04-20" } ``` --- ## Dialogs & Context Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/dialogs.md Build conversational flows using dialogs, context variables, and **webhooks**. Dialogs define how your bot understands and responds to user input. ## What is a dialog? A **dialog** is a conversation building block. It consists of: - **Triggers** — keywords or intents that activate the dialog (e.g., "order status", "track my package") - **Response** — what the bot says when the dialog is triggered - **Context variables** — data collected during the conversation (e.g., order number, email address) ## Key concepts | Concept | Description | | - | - | | **Dialogs** | Conversation building blocks that match user intent | | **Context variables** | Store and pass data between dialog turns | | **Transactional dialogs** | Perform actions (e.g., API calls) during conversation | | **Validation webhooks** | Validate user input in real-time | | **Language support** | Multi-language conversations | ## Context variable webhooks Enrich conversations by fetching external data via webhooks when context variables are set. For example, when a user provides their order number, fetch the order details from your system: ```json { "webhook_url": "https://yourapi.com/orders/lookup", "variable": "order_number", "method": "POST" } ``` ## Transactional dialogs Execute business logic during conversations — look up orders, check availability, or create bookings. Transactional dialogs call your API and use the response to continue the conversation. --- ## Set Up a Chatbot with Live Handover Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/guides/chatbot-live-handover.md Build a chatbot that answers common questions automatically and hands off to a human agent when it can't help. ## What you'll build A web chat bot that answers FAQs and seamlessly transfers to Agent Inbox when it can't resolve an issue. ## Prerequisites - A CM.com account with Conversational AI and Customer Engagement access - Web Chat configured on your website ## Step 1: Create dialog flows Set up dialogs in Conversational AI to handle your most common customer questions. ## Step 2: Configure escalation Add a dialog that detects when the bot can't answer and triggers a live agent handover via the Conversational Router. ## Step 3: Connect to Agent Inbox Configure the router to forward escalated conversations to Agent Inbox, where your support agents can take over. ## Next steps - [Conversational AI](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai) — chatbot documentation - [Agent Inbox](https://docs.cm.com/customer-engagement/agent-inbox) — helpdesk integration - [Chatbot & Routing](https://docs.cm.com/customer-engagement/chatbot-routing) — routing configuration --- ## Conversational AI Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai.md Build intelligent conversational experiences powered by [CM.com Halo](https://www.cm.com/halo). Automate customer interactions, create dialog flows, and deploy web chat on your website. ## Explore ## Quick links

Guides

Step-by-step guides to build your first AI-powered conversation.

Get Started
--- ## Web Chat Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/web-chat.md Add an AI-powered chat widget to your website. Web Chat provides a customizable floating widget with a JavaScript API for deep integration. ## Quick start Add the widget to any page with a single script tag: ```html ``` This renders a floating chat button in the bottom-right corner of your page. ## Key capabilities - **Floating widget** — drop-in chat widget for any website - **JavaScript API** — programmatic control over chat behavior - **Presence check** — detect if agents are available for live handover - **Page push** — proactively suggest pages based on conversation context - **Event triggers** — fire custom events from chat interactions - **Shared history** — maintain conversation history across page navigation - **FAQ integration** — surface knowledge base answers automatically ## JavaScript API Control the widget programmatically: ```javascript // Open the chat widget window.cmWebChat.open(); // Send a message programmatically window.cmWebChat.sendMessage("I need help with my order"); // Listen for events window.cmWebChat.on('message', (msg) => { console.log('New message:', msg); }); ``` --- ## Getting Started Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/guides/getting-started.md # Getting Started with Conversational AI Build a chatbot and put it on your website in three steps — create a dialog, add context, and deploy the Web Chat widget. ## Prerequisites - A CM.com account with Conversational AI access - Access to the Conversational AI dashboard ## Step 1: Create your first dialog A **dialog** is a conversation building block that matches user intent and returns a response. Create one in the Conversational AI dashboard, or check the API is reachable: ```bash curl -X GET https://api.cm.com/conversational/v1/health \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" ``` ```json { "status": "ok", "service": "conversational-ai", "version": "v1" } ``` In the dashboard: 1. Go to **Conversational AI > Dialogs** 2. Click **Create Dialog** 3. Define a greeting intent (e.g., keywords: "hello", "hi", "hey") 4. Add a response: "Hi! How can I help you today?" ## Step 2: Add context Use **context variables** to personalize conversations and maintain state across messages. For example, store the user's name and reference it in later responses. ## Step 3: Deploy Web Chat Add the web chat widget to your website with a single script tag: ```html ``` This renders a floating chat button on your site. Visitors can click it to start a conversation with your bot. ## Next steps - [Dialogs & Context](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/dialogs) — build conversation flows - [Web Chat](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/web-chat) — deploy chat on your website - [Connect](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/connect) — integrate with external systems --- ## Conversational AI API endpoints (v1) API reference: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-ai/v1/api-reference Base URL: `https://api.cm.com` ### GET /conversational/v1/health Health check Verify that the Conversational AI API is reachable and your credentials are valid. --- # Conversational Router > Router brings your conversations to the right destination—intelligently connecting all your chat applications into one seamless, unified platform. --- ## Conversational Router Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router.md Router brings your conversations to the right destination—intelligently connecting all your chat applications into one seamless, unified platform. Central Services is an umbrella name for a few applications that don't (primarily) provide client facing functionality but are providers of said functionalities to other products that are client facing. You can describe them as the platform on which the client facing products are build. ## Quick links - [Getting started](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started) --- ## Agent Inbox Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/agent-inbox.md ## Overview This application integrates Agent Inbox (formerly Robin) with the Conversational Router, allowing live agents to participate in routed conversations alongside bots and other services. Once connected, you can include Agent Inbox in your flows to support use cases such as bot-to-live-agent handover. For background information on Agent Inbox, see the Mobile Service Cloud documentation: [https://developers.cm.com/mobile-service-cloud/docs/msc](https://developers.cm.com/mobile-service-cloud/docs/msc) . ## Configuration This connector has two custom settings you must provide: - **Name**: application display name. Use a clear, descriptive label, so it’s easy to identify in flows and states. - **API key**: the project specific key designated to each Agent Inbox subscription. - **Environment**: to which application environment you want your messages to be routed. **Note**: this setting is only visible to CM employees. \[Agent Inbox settings] --- ## Applications Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications.md ## Overview Applications are the destinations of the Router: the services that handle conversations routed to them. The **Applications** page lists the applications connected to your account: - **Agent Inbox** — CM.com's contact center for live agents (see [Agent Inbox](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/agent-inbox)). - **AI cloud** — your Conversational AI Cloud bot (see [Conversational AI Cloud](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/conversation-ai-cloud)). - **HALO** — CM.com's agentic AI solution (see [HALO](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/halo)). - **Marketplace** — third-party contact center integrations (see [Marketplace](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/marketplace)). \[Applications overview] Each row shows the application's icon, name and identifying detail (such as the HALO profile or environment), and when and by whom it was last edited. ## Connecting an application Click **Connect application** and pick the application type. CM.com's own applications are listed first, followed by the Marketplace integrations provisioned on your account. Types with a one-per-account limit (Agent Inbox, AI cloud) are hidden from the list once connected. Each type has its own settings — for example, Agent Inbox requires its API key, and HALO requires selecting a profile. See the per-application pages for details and prerequisites. \[Application settings] ## Editing and deleting Click an application row (or its Actions menu → **Edit**) to change its settings; use the Actions menu's **Delete** to remove it, confirming in the dialog. > ❗️ Deleting an application > > Deletion is permanent and cannot be undone. An application that is still used by a published flow cannot be deleted — disconnect it from the flow first. ## Using applications in flows Applications become useful once they are connected to a flow and linked inside its states — that is where you define which conversations they receive (see [Flows](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows) and [States](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states)). --- ## Conversation AI Cloud Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/conversation-ai-cloud.md ## Overview The Conversational AI Cloud Application connects your Conversational AI Cloud projects to the Conversational Router, so your bot can participate in routed conversations alongside other services. Once added to a flow, the bot can receive customer messages, send replies, and hand over to a human agent when needed. For background information on Conversational AI Cloud, see documentation: [https://developers.cm.com/conversational-ai-cloud/docs/introduction](https://developers.cm.com/conversational-ai-cloud/docs/introduction) ## Configuration This application has one setting you can configure: - **Name**: application display name. Use a clear, descriptive label, so it’s easy to identify in flows and states. - **Environment**: to which application environment you want your messages to be routed. **Note**: this setting is only visible to CM employees. \[Conversational AI Cloud settings] --- ## HALO Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/halo.md ## Overview This application integrates HALO, CM.com's agentic AI solution, with the Conversational Router. HALO enables businesses to build AI agents that handle customer conversations across channels without requiring code. Once connected, you can include HALO in your flows to support use cases such as automated customer interactions, AI-assisted support, and bot-to-live-agent handover. For more information on HALO, see [https://knowledgecenter.cm.com/knowledge-center/halo](https://knowledgecenter.cm.com/knowledge-center/halo). ## Configuration This connector has two custom settings you must provide: - **Name**: application display name. Use a clear, descriptive label, so it’s easy to identify in flows and states. - **Profile**: the HALO profile to associate with this application. Available profiles are loaded from your account and determine how conversations are handled. - **Environment**: to which application environment you want your messages to be routed. **Note**: this setting is only visible to CM employees. \[HALO settings] --- ## Marketplace Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/marketplace.md ## Overview This application integrates Marketplace's live chat integrations with the Router. Marketplace enables businesses to connect services like Quandago and Salesforce to handle customer conversations. For more information on Marketplace, see [https://knowledgecenter.cm.com/knowledge-center/central-services/marketplace](https://knowledgecenter.cm.com/knowledge-center/central-services/marketplace). ## Configuration This connector has two custom settings you must provide: - **Name**: application display name. Use a clear, descriptive label, so it’s easy to identify in flows and states. - **Integration**: the Marketplace integration to associate with this application. Available integrations are loaded from your account. \[Marketplace settings] --- ## Business Messaging Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/business-messaging.md ## Overview Business Messaging connects the messaging channels available on your CM.com account to the Conversational Router, so those channels can participate in your flows. Once connected, inbound messages from your configured channels are routed through the Router according to your active state, and outbound replies are delivered back over the same channel(s). For background information on Business Messaging and supported channels, see the Messaging page: [https://developers.cm.com/messaging/docs/introduction](https://developers.cm.com/messaging/docs/introduction) ## Prerequisites To enable routing via the Conversational Router, set the Router as the message destination for each channel identifier you want to use. A channel identifier is the specific address to reach you within a messaging channel. Examples include: - **WhatsApp**: your WhatsApp Business phone number. - **SMS**: your long number or short code. - **Facebook Messenger**: your Facebook Page. Each channel identifier has a Destination setting that defines where inbound (customer-initiated) messages are delivered. To access that, navigate to [Channels](https://www.cm.com/app/channels/overview) and open the channel identifier you want to route through the Conversational Router. Then click the destination button shown on the page, select the Conversational Router in the overlay, and save. \[Add destination] \[Choose Conversational Router as a destination] After these settings are processed by all systems, incoming (MO) messages will be forwarded to the Conversational Router. ## Configuration After configuring your channel identifiers, open the [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview) page in your Router account and click **Connect channel**: \[Connect channel] You are shown two settings: - **Channel identifier**: a selection box with all the identifiers your account has in Channels. - **Name**: the display name. Use a clear, descriptive label so it's easy to identify in flows and states. Depending on the channel type there may be additional settings — for example, SMS and WhatsApp channels offer **Recall outreach**, which prepends the original outbound message to the conversation when a customer replies to a campaign, so agents have full context. > 🚧 Webhook registration > > Connecting a channel registers a new webhook for its identifier. If other webhooks are still configured for that channel, they may need to be removed manually to avoid duplicate message delivery. --- ## Channels Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview.md ## Overview Channels are the entry points of the Router: the messaging channels your customers use to reach you — WhatsApp, SMS, RCS, Facebook Messenger, Instagram, Email, Web Conversations, or a custom service speaking the [TwoWay](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-service) format. The **Channels** page lists all channels connected to your account and lets you organize them into groups. \[Channels overview] Each row shows the channel's name, its identifier (for example the phone number or sender address), and when and by whom it was last edited. Groups render as a parent row with their member channels nested beneath. You can search and sort the list. ## Connecting and buying channels The page header offers three actions: - **Connect channel** — connect a channel identifier that is already provisioned on your CM.com account. Pick the identifier, optionally give the channel a clear name, and configure any channel-specific settings. See the per-channel pages under [Connections](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/connections) for details and prerequisites. \[Connect channel] - **Buy channel** — a shortcut to acquiring new channel identifiers which will take you to the CM.com store; **Custom service** creates a connection for your own integration directly in the Router — see [Custom service](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-service). \[Buy channel] - **Create group** — organize channels into a group. \[Create channels group] > 🚧 Webhook registration > > Connecting a channel registers a new webhook for its identifier. If other webhooks are still configured for that channel, remove them manually to avoid duplicate message delivery. ## Editing a channel Click a channel row to edit it. Every channel has a **Name**; the remaining settings depend on the channel type — for example, SMS and WhatsApp offer a message-recall switch, Email has sender settings and an Implementation tab with your forwarding address, and a custom service has its message/event endpoints and implementation details. See the per-channel pages under [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview). \[Channel settings] ## Deleting a channel Open the channel's Actions menu (three dots) and choose **Delete**, then confirm. > 📘 Channels used by a flow > > A channel that is routed by a flow cannot be deleted — the option is disabled and a tooltip names the flow. Disconnect the channel from the flow first. > ❗️ Deleted channel recovery > > Once a channel is deleted it can't be recovered. ## Channel groups Groups let a single flow route several channels together — for example one "Support channels" group for your WhatsApp and SMS numbers. In a flow, a group counts as one connection; the Router fans messages out to the right member automatically. > 📘 Group behavior > > Grouping exists for configuration convenience; it does not change how individual conversations behave. A group must always keep at least one member. Deleting a group never deletes its channels. ### Create a group Click **Create group**, give the group a name, and tick the channels that should join. Only channels that are not in a group and not already routed by a flow can be added. \[Create group] ### Edit a group Click the group row (or its Actions menu → **Edit**) to rename the group or manage its members. Each member has a remove (×) button; a member channel's own settings are edited via that channel's row, not in the group. \[Edit group] ### Ungrouping and removing members - A group's Actions menu offers **Ungroup**: the group is dissolved and its channels remain as individual channels. \[Ungroup the group] - A member row's Actions menu offers **Remove from group**. \[Remove channel from the group] - An ungrouped channel's Actions menu offers **Add to group**. \[Add channel to the group] > 🚧 Groups routed by a flow > > When a group is routed by a flow, destructive actions are restricted: the group cannot be ungrouped, flow-routed channels cannot be added to a group, and removing a member from the group asks for confirmation — the removal changes which channels the flow routes. --- ## Custom service Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-service.md ## Overview A **Custom service** is a generic connector that lets you integrate your own service with the Conversational Router - even if there isn’t a ready-made adapter. Using the TwoWay JSON protocol, your service can receive messages and session events from the Router and send them back through the platform, enabling full bidirectional interaction like any other application. ## Configuration To be able to receive messages you must have a publicly accessible webhook configured. \[Fill out the URL to your message webhook here] During a session events will come by. Events can be seen as metadata about a conversation, giving information not on the content that is shared but in what context that is being done. Being notified about these events can be achieved by filling out the events endpoint. \[Fill out the URL to your events webhook here] When application is created, you can see implementation details needed to integrate. \[Custom service connection implementation details] --- ## Email Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/email.md ## Overview The Email application enables email as a conversational channel within the Router. It supports both inbound (receiving) and outbound (sending) emails. ## Configuration For this application you can configure in the **Settings** tab: - **Name**: application display name. Use a clear, descriptive label, so it's easy to identify in flows and states. - **Sender email**: the email address used when sending outbound emails. Select a domain from the dropdown and enter the local part (e.g., `support`). The available domains are configured on your account in the [Email Gateway application](https://www.cm.com/en-gb/app/email). - **Sender name**: the display name shown to recipients in outbound emails (e.g., "Customer Support"). - **Integration mode**: when enabled, outbound emails are routed through the full pipeline but delivered to a test inbox instead of the actual recipient. Useful for verifying your integration without sending real emails. \[Email settings] > 🚧 Integration mode billing > > Messages sent in integration mode are still billed. In the **Implementation** tab you can find the forwarding email address, which is automatically generated when the application is created. Several Email applications can share the same forwarding address, as long as each has a different sender email. An inbound email is then delivered to the application whose sender email appears in the email's **To** recipients, or failing that in its **Cc** recipients (the first match wins). The combination of forwarding address and sender email must be unique within your account. > Shared forwarding address > > When applications share a forwarding address, an email addressed to none of their sender emails cannot be attributed and is not processed. Make sure the redirected mailbox address is the sender email of exactly one application. \[Email implementation details] ### Inbound email #### Email redirection setup To receive emails in the Router, you must configure an email redirect from your business email address to the forwarding email address. This ensures that emails sent to your public-facing address (e.g., [support@yourcompany.com](mailto\:support@yourcompany.com)) are redirected to the Router for processing. > 🚧 Inbound email redirection > > You must use redirect rule, not forward. Redirecting preserves the original sender information and email headers, which is required for the Email application to correctly identify the sender. The redirection setup depends on your email provider. Consult your provider's documentation for instructions on configuring email redirect rules. #### CC recipients When a customer sends an email with CC recipients, those addresses are forwarded to the routed conversation so the agent (or downstream application) sees who else is on the thread. > 📘 BCC is never available on inbound > > Mail protocol limitation: SMTP relays strip BCC headers before delivery. The Router only sees what the receiving mailbox sees, so BCC recipients on inbound emails are not visible. ### Outbound email When a contact center agent replies to a conversation, the Router sends the response as an email to the original sender using the configured sender email and sender name. --- ## Web Conversations Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/web-conversations.md ## Overview The Web Conversations application connects your website’s chat widget to the Conversational Router so website visitors can join the same routed conversations as your other applications. For product details, see the Web Conversations documentation: [https://developers.cm.com/conversational-ai-cloud/docs/getting-started-with-web-conversations](https://developers.cm.com/conversational-ai-cloud/docs/getting-started-with-web-conversations) ## Configuration This application has one setting you can configure: - **Name**: application display name. Use a clear, descriptive label, so it’s easy to identify in flows and states. - **Configuration**: your Web Conversations configuration to associate with this app. Available configurations are loaded from your account. > 📘 Advanced settings availability > > Advanced settings are only available to CM employees. \[Web Conversations settings] --- ## Connections Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/connections.md ## Overview Connections are the integration points that connect CM.com or third-party services to the Conversational Router. Each connection encapsulates the details and behavior required to exchange messages. By standardizing these concerns, connections let you plug services into your flows without re-implementing integration logic for each use case. We provide two ways to integrate: - **Ready-made connections**: prebuilt connectors for popular services. These minimize setup — often only basic configuration is needed, and credentials are required only when the service demands them — so you can start routing messages quickly. - **Custom integrations** via the [Custom service](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-service) connection: use this when you want to connect your own service or a system we don't offer out of the box. It enables bidirectional exchange of both messages and events with the Router, so you can participate in the same ecosystem as our ready-made integrations. Connections come in two kinds, mirroring their role in a flow, and each kind has its own management page in the Router: - **[Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview)** — the entry points customers message you on. Channels can be organized into groups. - [Business Messaging](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/business-messaging) (WhatsApp, SMS, RCS, Facebook Messenger, Instagram) - [Email](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/email) - [Custom service](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-service) - [Web Conversations](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/web-conversations) - **[Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications)** — the destinations conversations are routed to. - [Agent Inbox](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/agent-inbox) - [Conversational AI Cloud](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/conversation-ai-cloud) - [HALO](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/halo) - [Marketplace](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/marketplace) ## Prerequisites Most connections have minimal prerequisites: ensure the relevant product is added and active in Orders so the Router can deliver traffic to that connection. Business Messaging channels must be provisioned in the Channels product first — each connection's page above lists its specific prerequisites. ## Management - To add, edit, group, or delete a **channel**, see the [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview) page. - To add, edit, or delete an **application**, see the [Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications) page. > 🚧 Deleting connections used by a flow > > A connection that is routed by a flow can't be deleted. Chat ID is the stable identifier for a chat between one end user and one service identity on a single messaging channel. It represents the long‑lived thread linking the same participants on the same channel across time. This differs from `routerSessionId`, which identifies a single, finite interaction within that chat (for example, one support session that starts and ends). A single chat ID can span multiple `routerSessionId`s and is useful for grouping conversations historically and operationally. ## Concept and composition ### What defines a chat A chat is defined by the trio of channel, client, and host. The channel is the specific channel over which messages are exchanged. The client is the end user’s identifier on that channel (the client id), and the host is the service identity the user is talking to on that channel (the host id). ### Inputs and rationale Chat ID is derived from these three inputs: channel, client id, and host id. Including the channel is essential because the same user–service pair can exist across different channels; for instance, the same two phone numbers can converse via SMS and via WhatsApp, and those must be treated as distinct chats. Client and host identifiers always follow the addressing scheme of the channel you are using - for example, 1645 phone number for WhatsApp and SMS or an Instagram Scoped User ID (IGSID) for Instagram. Calling channels carry one exception: an anonymous caller has no number to be addressed by, so the client id is a per-call value instead. Each anonymous call is therefore its own chat, rather than every anonymous caller to the same number sharing one. Email is the other exception: an email thread, not the pair of addresses, is the conversation, so each thread has its own chat ID that cannot be computed from channel, client id and host id. Take it from the payloads you receive (or from the outbound-session response) and send it back as `chat.id`; the chat ID construction endpoint rejects the Email channel. ### Uniqueness and scope Chat ID is deterministic and unique for the combination of channel, client id, and host id. The same inputs always produce the same identifier, making chat ID a reliable key to group messages and sessions for the same participants on the same channel. Router account ID is not part of this calculation; in the rare case that two accounts share the same host identity on the same channel, the chat ID will be the same across those accounts. If any of the three inputs change - such as migrating to a new host number - a new chat ID is produced and will not automatically link back to the previous one. ### Relationship to router session ID Use chat ID to group sessions and retrieve history across time for the same participants on the same channel, while `routerSessionId` identifies a single finite session. You will receive both identifiers in the payloads TwoWay sends. Chat ID can be used for long‑term grouping and analytics, `routerSessionId` for session‑specific actions and history queries. ### Obtaining chat ID You will receive chat ID in platform payloads whenever you interact with the Router. This is the preferred way to use it because it ensures consistency across systems and avoids local differences in identifier formatting. If you need the platform to compute the identifier for a given combination of channel, client id, and host id call [this control API endpoint](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/routing-control-api#chat-id-construction). --- ## Configuration APIs Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/configuration-apis.md ## Overview The Router relies on several underlying settings that determine how messages are delivered, which endpoints are invoked, and how your channels are connected. This page documents the APIs you can use to inspect those configurations. When calling our APIs we require an authentication token to be present. Please refer to our [authentication page](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started#authentication) for details. ## Endpoints ### Router version installations This endpoint returns what versions of the router are configured on your account. In practice, you will: - Expose one or more webhooks to receive messages and session events from the Router. - Send outbound messages and events to the [TwoWay](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api#sending-messages) endpoint for your TwoWay application(s). - Adhere to the [TwoWay](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api#format) message schema for all inbound and outbound payloads. - Authenticate API calls as described in the [Authentication](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started#authentication) documentation. --- ## History API Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/history-api.md ## Overview Conversation History lets you retrieve the full record of a single session so you can review past messages, power support workflows, or run analytics. You request history by providing the `routerSessionId`. This identifier is included with Router traffic, for example when routing messages or events. The API can return just messages, messages with session events, or only events - depending on your query parameters. You can also request a summary in the response metadata and, if needed, delete a session’s history. A separate, paged endpoint is also available to fetch a conversation's transcript on demand, optionally transformed through a configured pipeline (for example to translate it into a language of your choice). When calling our APIs we require an authentication token to be present. Please refer to our [authentication page](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started#authentication) for details. ## Endpoints ### Get session history This API also supports retrieving [session events](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api#events) - you can include events with messages by adding the `includeEvents=true` query parameter. You can also only fetch events without messages by adding the `includeMessages=false` query parameter. This endpoint also allows you to fetch conversation history including a summary by setting `includeSummary=true`. You can also specify the language in which the summary should be and the maximum length. **Endpoint**: `GET https://api.cm.com/router/conversation-history/v1/accounts/{accountId}/session-history?routerSessionId={sessionId}&includeEvents={true/false}&includeMessages={true/false}&includeSummary={true/false}&summaryLanguage={lan}&maxSummaryLength={length}` **Header**: `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` **Permission**: `ConversationalRouter.SessionHistory_Read` | Field | Type | Description | | - | - | - | | accountId | Guid | The ID of logical account | | routerSessionId | Guid | Identifier of the session | | includeEvents | boolean | When true, session events are included in the response alongside messages. Default value is false | | includeMessages | boolean | When false, messages are omitted and only events are returned. Default value is true | | includeSummary | boolean | When true, a summary of the conversation is included in the response metadata. Default value is false | | summaryLanguage | string | The language the summary should be generated in. Requires `includeSummary=true` | | maxSummaryLength | int | The maximum length of the summary. Default value is 20 | > 📘 Setting parameters > > `includeEvents` and `includeMessages` cannot both be `false` — at least one must be requested, otherwise the endpoint returns `400 Bad Request`. Setting `summaryLanguage` without `includeSummary=true` also returns `400`. When the session has no stored history, the endpoint returns `204 No Content`. **Response body** | Field | Type | Description | | - | - | - | | accountId | Guid | The ID of the logical account | | sessionId | Guid | Identifier of the session. Also returned as `conversationId` (the same value) | | chatId | Guid | The hashed ID of the chat the session belongs to | | conversationHistory | array | The messages and/or events for that session, in the TwoWay [conversationMessages / conversationEvents](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api#format) format | | metadata | object | Metadata about the session history (see below) | Metadata properties: | Field | Type | Description | | - | - | - | | summary | string | A summary of the conversation’s text messages. Also returned as `conversationIds` (the same values) | When the chat has no recorded sessions, the endpoint returns `204 No Content`. ### Get conversation transcription This endpoint returns a conversation's full transcript as a chronological, paged list of messages, intended for handing a conversation over to a human agent or another system - for example when escalating a bot conversation, or archiving it. Optionally, each message can be run through a configured pipeline before it is returned by setting `transformWithPipelineId` - for example a translation pipeline, so you can fetch an on-demand transcript in a language of your choice by also setting `hostLanguage`. Per-message pipeline enrichment (detected language, extracted entities, sentiment, translation, redactions) is omitted by default; set `includeEnrichment=true` to include it. **Endpoint**: `GET https://api.cm.com/router/conversation-history/v2/accounts/{accountId}/conversations/{conversationId}/transcription?transformWithPipelineId={pipelineId}&hostLanguage={lan}&includeEnrichment={true/false}&cursor={cursor}` **Header**: `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` **Permission**: `ConversationalRouter.SessionHistory_Read` | Field | Type | Description | | - | - | - | | accountId | Guid | The ID of logical account | | conversationId | Guid | Identifier of the conversation. ID of a configured pipeline to run over each message before it is returned, for example a translation pipeline. Omit to get the plain transcript | | hostLanguage | string | Optional. Overrides the pipeline's translation target language for this call (e.g. `nl`, `en`). Only meaningful together with `transformWithPipelineId`; ignored when the pipeline has no translation step | | includeEnrichment | boolean | Optional. When true, includes per-message pipeline enrichment (detected language, extracted entities, sentiment, translation, redactions) on each message. Default value is false | | cursor | string | Optional. E.g. for WhatsApp that's the phone number, for Instagram it is the Instagram Scoped User ID (IGSID). ### Ensure session Ensure that a routing session exists for the given client, host, and channel. If no session exists, it is created; if it exists, a current session ID is returned. **Endpoint**: `POST https://api.cm.com/router/control/v1/accounts/{LogicalAccountId}/routing/ensure-session` **Header**: `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` **Permissions**: `ConversationalRouter.RouterSession_Update` **Request body**: ```json { "ClientId":"{ClientId}", "HostId":"{HostId}", "Channel":"{Channel}" } ``` | Field | Description | Required | | - | - | - | | LogicalAccountId | The ID of logical account | Yes | | Channel | The channel over which messages are sent | Yes | | ClientId | The client id from which messages are sent | Yes | | HostId | The host id to which messages are sent | Yes | The client and host IDs correspond to the identifiers of the channel that is used. E.g. for WhatsApp that's the phone number, for Instagram it is the Instagram Scoped User ID (IGSID). ### Create outbound session Creates a session for outbound initiated messages (outreach) using (for example) WhatsApp templates. Changes to the appropriate outbound state if necessary. This API provides information like the `applicationId` you'll need to send messages to our TwoWay API. Currently useful for Agent Inbox. Get in touch with us for custom integrations. **Endpoint**: `POST https://api.cm.com/router/control/v1/accounts/{LogicalAccountId}/outbound-session` **Header**: `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` **Permissions**: `ConversationalRouter.RouterSession_Update` **Request body**: ```json { "SourceComponent": "AgentInbox", "Channel": "{{Channel}}", "ConversationHostId": "{{ConversationHostId}}", "ConversationClientId": "{{ConversationClientId}}", "ForceNewSession": false } ``` | Field | Description | Required | | - | - | - | | SourceComponent | The source component to look up for message routing | Yes | | Channel | The channel over which messages are sent | Yes | | ConversationHostId | The client id from which messages are sent | Yes | | ConversationClientId | The host id to which messages are sent | Yes | | ForceNewSession | When true, ends any existing session and starts a new one. Defaults to false. On the Email channel every call opens a new thread regardless of this value: a business-initiated email is a new thread by nature, and there is no way to name an existing one here. Reply into an existing email thread through the TwoWay API with that thread's `chat.id` instead | No | **Response body**: ```json { "SourceApplicationId": "SomeApplicationId", "ChatId": "{{ChatId}}", "SessionId": "{{SessionId}}", "StateId": "{{StateId}}" } ``` Send the returned `ChatId` back as `chat.id` on the first message you post to the TwoWay API. For Email this is what threads the message into the conversation just created; the customer's reply then continues that same chat. | Field | Description | | - | - | | SourceApplicationId | Application ID to use when sending your outbound message to TwoWay | | ChatId | A hash created from the combination of client id, host id and channel. For more information, see [Chat ID construction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/chatid-construction) | | SessionId | The ID generated for your new session | | StateId | ID of the state which is configured to receive the message | --- ## TwoWay API Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api.md ## Overview TwoWay is a JSON-based format the Router uses to exchange data with external services. It defines a consistent envelope and payloads for both messages and events, so your custom service can participate in routed conversations just like any built‑in application. With TwoWay, you use the same contract across channels (for example, WhatsApp, SMS, Web Conversations). ## Integration ### Prerequisites Before start, make sure you have created TwoWay application. For all the details on how to create and configure it, see section [TwoWay](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-service). ### Sending messages To send data into the Router, POST TwoWay-formatted JSON to your TwoWay application’s inbound URL. You can copy the exact endpoint from your application from the frontend (the **Copy Inbound URL** action) or construct it yourself based on the info in the messages you're receiving. Include authentication on every request (see [Authentication](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started#authentication)). Payloads must conform to the TwoWay schema which is described in section [Format](#format). What happens next: 1. The Router validates your payload and routes it according to the currently active state in the relevant flow. 2. Depending on your flow and active state, messages can be delivered to one or more applications. 3. The Router may add metadata like `targetApplicationInfo` when delivering to downstream applications, providing the info for talking back #### Example Below is an example for sending a simple text message through the SMS channel. To see all available message types, please see section [Message types](#message-types). **Endpoint**: `POST https://api.cm.com/router/twoway/v1/accounts/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/applications/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` **Header**: `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` **Request body**: ```json { "chat": { "accountId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "channel": "SMS", "conversationClientId": "+31600000000", "conversationHostId": "+31611111111", }, "conversationMessages": [ { "$type": "text", "text": "Hello", } ] } ``` ### Receiving messages To receive data from the Router, implement an HTTPS JSON webhook. The Router will POST TwoWay-formatted requests to your message (and optionally events) endpoint(s). Your service should: - Accept `POST` requests with `application/json`. - Allowlist the Router's outbound IP range in your firewall if necessary (see [Whitelisting](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started#whitelisting)). ## Format TwoWay defines a single, consistent envelope for everything the Conversational Router exchanges with your service. Every payload has the same top level and then carries either messages or events. This makes it easy to parse and to build logic that works across connections. There are two payload kinds: - **conversationMessages**: The payload contains one or more messages (text, media, location, etc.). - **conversationEvents**: The payload contains one or more events (for example, a session ended, a client left/rejoined, or an agent was assigned). ### Base Every TwoWay payload includes three parts: - `chat:` identifiers and context for the conversation (who is involved, on which channel) - `conversationMessages` or `conversationEvents`: the content of the message/event. - `targetApplicationInfo` (added by the Router on delivery): metadata containing the ID of the application to which the router routed the message. **chat** property: | Field | Description | Required | | - | - | - | | id | A hash created from the combination of client id, host id and channel | Yes | | sessionId | The id for the current session | No | | accountId | The id of logical account | Yes | | channel | The medium being used for communication, e.g. WhatsApp or CXWebConversations | Yes | | conversationClientId | The client id from which messages are sent | Yes | | conversationHostId | The host id to which messages are sent | Yes | | conversationClientName | The display name of the client on the channel | No | **conversationMessages** or **conversationEvents** properties: described in sections [Events](#events) and [Messages](#messages). **targetApplicationInfo** property: an object containing information about the application to which the `conversationMessages`/`conversationEvents` were sent. It is added automatically by the Conversational Router. | Field | Description | | - | - | | applicationId | The id of the target application | ### Events Events communicate context and lifecycle information around a conversation rather than message content. They help participants understand what’s happening (for example, a session ended, a client became inactive, or an agent joined). #### Base All events share these generic fields: | Field | Description | Required | | - | - | - | | $type | The type of the message, see [Event types](#event-types) | Yes | | id | The id of the event | No | | createdOn | The timestamp (UTC) at which the event was created within the Conversational Router | No | | channelNativeReference | A channelNativeId of a previous message, to which is replied | No | > **NOTE**: we do not support setting `channelNativeId` on events, so you can only refer to messages using `channelNativeReference`. #### Event types ##### Router events Emitted to inform you about Router-specific lifecycle changes (e.g., `RouterSessionEnded`). These are not accepted as inbound payloads to TwoWay; you receive them on your configured events webhook in the TwoWay application. ###### RouterSessionStarted Notifies you of the fact that the router session has been started for a certain chat ```json { "chat": { "id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "sessionId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "accountId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "channel": "WhatsApp", "conversationClientId": "+316012345678", "conversationHostId": "00316012345678", "conversationClientName": null }, "conversationEvents": [ { "$type": "routerSessionStarted", "Reason": "reason", "Context" : {} } ] } ``` | Field | Description | Required | | - | - | - | | Reason | Reason for the session initialization | Yes | | Context | Dictionary containing extra information passed along with the initialization | No | ###### RouterSessionEnded Notifies you of the fact that the router session has been reset for a certain chat ```json { "chat": { "id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "sessionId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "accountId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "channel": "WhatsApp", "conversationClientId": "+316012345678", "conversationHostId": "00316012345678", "conversationClientName": null }, "conversationEvents": [ { "$type": "routerSessionEnded", "Reason": "reason", "Context" : {} } ] } ``` | Field | Description | Required | | - | - | - | | Reason | Reason for the session termination | Yes | | Context | Dictionary containing extra information passed along with the termination | No | ###### ApplicationRoutingActivated Notifies the application receiving this event that messages and/or events will be sent its way from then on (according to the current state) ```json { "chat": { "id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "sessionId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "accountId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "channel": "WhatsApp", "conversationClientId": "+316012345678", "conversationHostId": "00316012345678", "conversationClientName": null }, "conversationEvents": [ { "$type": "applicationRoutingActivated", "Context" : {} } ] } ``` | Field | Description | Required | | -
