Use it to verify that your flows, states, and pipelines behave as intended, and to investigate individual conversations. \[Explorer] ## Browsing and searching - **Browse**: with an empty search box, the list shows conversations ordered by recent activity, loading more as you scroll. - **Search**: typing a query switches the list to a ranked full-text search across message content. Filters work in both modes: - **Date range** — limit results to a period. - **Channel** — one or more channels (WhatsApp, SMS, RCS, Facebook Messenger, Instagram, Email). - **Engagement** — by default only engaged conversations are shown (**Only engaged conversations**); switch to **All conversations** to include sessions where the customer never sent a message (for example, web-widget page loads). - Via the **+** menu you can add filters on **Flow**, **State**, **Application**, **Client ID**, and **Conversation ID**, and clear all filters. ## Transcript Selecting a conversation opens its transcript: customer and application messages as chat bubbles, with lifecycle events (such as session start) shown as dividers between them. The header shows the conversation ID (with a copy button) and the time of the first and last message. \[Transcript with routing detail] Every routed inbound message carries a **routing disclosure** — expand it to see: - the flow and state that handled the message, - the destination(s) it was routed to, - for each destination: the text that was actually delivered (when a pipeline transformed it), the pipeline steps that ran (for example language identification and translation) with their outcomes, and whether a guard step blocked delivery. This is the place to verify [pipeline](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines) behaviour end to end: for example, a Dutch inbound message translated to English before delivery to your bot shows the original text in the bubble and the translated text in the destination card. ## Settings The **Settings** button opens the history settings: - **Retention period** — how long conversation history is stored: **30 days** or **Do not retain**. When set to "Do not retain", no history is recorded for your account and the Explorer stays empty. \[History settings] ## API access The **API access** button shows what you need to query conversation history programmatically: - your product token (masked, with a copy action), and - a ready-made example request against the conversation history API. \[History API access] See the [Conversation History API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/history-api) page for the full API reference. --- ## Flows Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows.md ## Overview A flow defines how messages are routed through the Conversational Router for a given use case (for example, bot-first with handover to an agent). Each flow is composed of one or more states. You design a flow in the editor by connecting channels and applications and configuring states with directional links. When a flow is published, new conversations start in its default state, and you can transition to other states in real time (for example, from bot to agent). ## Management You can manage your flows on the Flows page. \[Flows overview] The list shows each flow's name and description, the connected channels and applications, its status (**Published** or **Draft**), and when and by whom it was last edited. You can search flows by name or description and sort by name or last edited. ### Add flow Click the **Add flow** button. You will be redirected to the flow editor, where you can configure it. Please see the [Configuration](#configuration) section for more information. ### Edit flow Click a flow in the list, or open its Actions menu (three dots) and choose **Edit**. ### Publish and unpublish from the list The Actions menu also lets you **Publish** a draft flow or **Unpublish** a published one without opening the editor. See [Publishing](#publishing) for the requirements. ### Delete flow Open the flow's Actions menu (three dots) and choose **Delete**, then confirm the deletion in the dialog. > ❗️ Deleting a flow > > Deletion is permanent and cannot be undone. Ensure the flow is no longer needed before proceeding. > A published flow cannot be deleted. To delete it, first unpublish the flow. ## Configuration The flow editor is a single page where you design how conversations are routed: \[Flow editor] - The **name** and **description** are edited inline at the top of the page. Use a clear name and an optional description that states the purpose (for example, "Support – bot first, agent fallback"). - The **States** card is where you build the routing itself — see the [States](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states) page for the concept and detailed guidance. - The right-hand rail holds the flow's **Channels**, **Applications**, and **Conversation timeout** settings. Your work is saved explicitly: the **Save** button stores your changes as a draft without affecting the published state, and **Discard changes** reverts them. If you navigate away with unsaved changes, the editor asks whether to save or discard them. ### Channels and applications Before you can use a channel or application inside a state, it must be connected to the flow. Use the **Add** buttons in the **Channels** and **Applications** sections of the editor's right-hand rail. Only connected channels, channel groups, and applications appear in the state editor. - **Channels** route incoming messages through the flow's states. You can connect an individual channel or a channel group (see [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview)); a group counts as a single connection that fans out to its members. - **Applications** are the destinations messages can be routed to within states (for example Agent Inbox or an AI bot — see [Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications)). > 📘 Connecting channels > > A channel (or group) can be connected to only one flow at a time. If a channel is unavailable in the Add list, it is already connected to another flow. > 🚧 Disconnecting a channel or application > > If a connection is used by a link in any state of this flow, removing it also removes those links. Save is blocked for a published flow while a state has no links left. ### Conversation timeout The **Conversation timeout** setting determines how long a conversation stays active after the last message. When the timeout is reached, the conversation is automatically closed and a new incoming message starts a fresh session. Choose between **1 hour**, **4 hours**, **1 day** (default), **1 week**, and **30 days** — for example, pick 30 days when your customer service follows up on a ticket over several weeks and you want the conversation to stay open. ### States States are edited directly inside the flow editor: each state is a tab, and its routes are listed as a table — pick a source and a target to create a route. For detailed guidance, see the [States](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states) page. ## Publishing When you are ready to route traffic through a configured flow, publish it. Publishing makes the flow active: new messages are routed through it, starting in its default state. Click the **Publish** button in the editor (or in the list's Actions menu) and confirm. After publishing, the flow's status changes to **Published**. > 📘 Publish requirements > > A flow can only be published when its configuration is complete: it must have a name, at least two connected channels/applications, at least one state, a default state, and every state must have at least one link. Any unsaved changes must be saved first. The Publish button's tooltip tells you which requirement is still missing. If you need to deactivate a flow, **Unpublish** it. Unpublishing stops it from routing new messages. After confirming, the flow's status changes back to **Draft**. > 🚧 Editing a published flow > > You can keep editing a published flow, but saving re-validates the configuration — for example, you cannot save a published flow with a state that has no links. --- ## Getting started Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/getting-started.md ## Concepts ### Chat vs session Understanding the difference between a chat and a session is essential. - **Chat**: a chat refers to the communication between both end-user to end-user and end-user to automated system (even automated system to automated system) on a single messaging channel. It is a long-lived thread that connects the same participants on the same channel. - **Session**: a session, on the other hand, is a single, finite interaction within that chat. Essentially, a single chat can contain multiple sessions. For more detailed information, visit the [Chat ID construction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/chatid-construction) page. #### Chat ID The chat ID is a key concept to understand, as it uniquely identifies a chat and is used throughout this documentation. It is constructed using three components: channel, client ID and host ID. For more details on these components, refer to the [Chat ID construction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/chatid-construction) page. > 📘 Chat ID reversibility > > The chat ID is not reversible, meaning you cannot extract the channel, client, or host IDs from it. However, this is not necessary, as these fields are included in the payload sent via TwoWay. > > Additionally, there is an API available for constructing chat IDs — see the [Chat ID construction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/chatid-construction) page. ### Router components The key components of the Router are channels, applications, flows and states. #### Channels Channels are the entry points of the Router: the messaging channels your customers use to reach you. They are managed on the [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview) page. CM's communication channels are provided by Business Messaging; a custom service can act as a channel through the [TwoWay API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api). #### Applications Applications are the destinations of the Router: ready-made connections such as a bot or an agent inbox that handle routed conversations. They are managed on the [Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications) page; see [Connections](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/connections) for the catalog. #### Flows A flow defines how messages are routed through the Conversational Router for a given use case (see the [Flows](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows) page). #### States A state is a distinct phase within a flow that determines how messages are routed at a given moment (see the [States](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states) page). ## APIs We have several APIs that can be used for custom integrations: - **TwoWay API**. TwoWay is a JSON-based format the Conversational Router uses to exchange data with external services. Use the TwoWay API to connect your service to the Conversational Router. Read more about it on the [TwoWay API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/twoway-api) page. - **Conversation history API**. Conversation History lets you retrieve the full record of a single session, enabling you to review past messages, support workflows, or run analytics. Find more information on the [Conversation History API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/history-api) page. - **Routing control API**. This API allows you to modify a conversation's behavior at runtime. For more details see the [Routing control API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/routing-control-api) page. - **Configuration API**. This API lets you retrieve the configurations you have set up for the Router. Learn more on the [Configuration APIs](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/configuration-apis) page. ## Authentication All Conversational Router API requests require authentication to ensure data security and prevent misuse. Authentication involves product token: a credential used to authenticate API requests, included in the `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN` header (e.g., `X-CM-PRODUCTTOKEN: {your_product_token}`). You can retrieve it in the Router: open the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer) and click **API access** to view your product token together with a ready-made example request. When configuring a custom service, the same credentials are shown on the connection's **Implementation** tab. > ❗️ Product token security > > It is crucial to keep product tokens secure, as they grant permissions associated with your account. Do not share them with anyone to prevent unauthorized access. ## Channels The CM.com messaging platform supports a wide variety of channels. You can find a list of supported channels and a compatibility matrix on the [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels) page under Custom integration. To route messages through the Business Messaging application, you first need to configure channels in the Channels platform. For each channel identifier, select Router as the message destination. For more details, refer to the Prerequisites section on the [Business Messaging](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/business-messaging) page. ## Onboarding When using the Router for the first time, you can take advantage of the onboarding wizard to quickly set up connections and flows. The wizard simplifies the initial configuration process, allowing you to get started with minimal effort. For detailed instructions and additional information, refer to the [Onboarding](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/onboarding) page. ## Whitelisting If your endpoints only accept traffic from known addresses, allow the Router's outbound IP range **85.119.48.0/21** so we can deliver your messages. Allow the whole range: the individual addresses the Router sends from can change within it. --- ## Home Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/home.md ## Overview Home is the Router's dashboard: a snapshot of the past 7 days of routed traffic, so you can see at a glance whether messages are flowing and where they go. \[Home dashboard] ## What you see ### Key metrics Three cards summarize the last 7 days, each with a daily breakdown and a comparison against the preceding 7 days: - **Conversations** — the number of conversations routed. - **Inbound messages** — messages received from your customers. - **Outbound messages** — messages sent back to your customers. ### Conversation flow The **Conversation flow** card shows how conversations entered and moved between states: each row is a transition (for example, _New conversation → Bot support_, or _Bot support → Agent handover_) with the number and share of conversations that took it. Use the flow selector to focus on a single flow. This is a quick way to see, for example, what percentage of conversations get handed over from your bot to live agents. ### Traffic breakdown - **Messages per channel** — inbound and outbound volume per channel type (WhatsApp, SMS, Email, …). - **Routed to** — inbound messages delivered per destination application, so you can see how much traffic your bot handles versus your agents. The dashboard counts engaged conversations only — sessions where the customer never sent a message (such as web-widget page loads) are excluded. For inspecting individual conversations, use the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer). --- ## API breaking changes Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/api-breaking-changes.md ## Overview The new model centers on state-based routing: instead of issuing “routing mutations,” you design routing in your flow’s states and switch the active state at runtime. As part of this update, some endpoints were deprecated or revised, paths were adjusted, and new controls were introduced for managing session state. ## General ### Base URL change The full base URL follows the pattern `https://api.cm.com/{base-path}/accounts`. | API | V1 Base Path | V2 Base Path | | - | - | - | | Control API | conversational/control | router/control | | Configuration API | conversational/configuration | router/configuration | ## Business Messaging ingress API ### URL change **V1**: `conversational/router/v1/message-receivers/business-messaging/accounts/{accountId}/{messages|events}` **V2**: `router/businessmessaging/v1/accounts/{accountId}/{messages|events}` ## Configuration API ### Removed endpoint #### Retrieve BM webhook URL `GET v1/logical-accounts/{LogicalAccountId}/webhook-url` #### Get message recall identifiers `GET v1/accounts/{LogicalAccountId}/message-recall-identifiers` ## Control API ### Removed Endpoints #### Routing Mutation Requests `POST v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/routing/mutationrequests` This functionality has been removed. Model routing in flow states and switch the active state instead of issuing mutation requests. #### Get Router Chat Target Adapter `GET v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/rules/{ruleId}/targets` This functionality has been removed. Target selection now is determined by your configured state links. #### Invoke Command `POST v1/accounts/{logicalAccountId}/chats/{chatId}/commands` Use state changes to alter routing; command-based mutations are no longer supported. #### Add position request `POST v1/accounts/{logicalAccountId}/sessions/positionrequests` This functionality has been removed since Router V2 will not support Scripted Chatbot. ### Modified Endpoints #### Reset Router **V1**: `POST v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/routing/reset` **V2**: `PUT v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/session/end` **Changes**: HTTP method (POST → PUT), path change. #### Get Router State **V1**: `GET v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/routing` **V2**: `GET v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/session` **Changes**: path change. #### Ensure New Session **V1**: `POST v1/accounts/{accountId}/routing/ensure-new-session` ```json { "clientId": "string", "hostId": "string", "channel": "string" } ``` **V2**: `POST v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/session/new` ```json { "clientId": "string", "hostId": "string", "channel": "string", "reason": "string", "context": [ { "key": "value" } ], "sourceApplicationId": "guid" } ``` **Changes**: path change, request body. ### New Endpoints #### Set Active State Name `PUT v1/accounts/{accountId}/chats/{chatId}/session/state` ```json { "NewStateNameId": "string", "context": { "key": "value" } } ``` Sets the active state for a chat session at runtime, immediately updating how messages are routed. Use this in place of V1 routing mutations/commands. You can receive the configured states for an account using the following API call: `GET /api/configuration/v1/accounts/{accountId}/state-names` --- ## Migration from V1 to V2 Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/migration-from-v1-to-v2.md ## Summary V1 is now in maintenance mode, while V2 is the actively supported release with ongoing development. We recommend migrating to V2 to benefit from continued updates and improvements. To help with your migration, see the following pages: - [Setup comparisons](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/setup-comparisons): understand the differences in configuration models and see how common scenarios are set up in each version. - [API breaking changes](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/api-breaking-changes): review the API changes that may affect your integrations. ## How V1 and V2 coexist V1 and V2 run independently — configuring V2 does **not** automatically disable or "take over" from V1. Which router handles a conversation is determined by the **webhook registered on the channel**: a channel is routed by V2 only once its inbound webhook points at V2. Because of this: - You can build out your **entire V2 configuration ahead of time** — accounts, applications, flows, states, and handover settings — **without affecting live V1 traffic**. No messages reach V2 until you repoint a channel's webhook. - If a channel has **both** a V1 and a V2 webhook registered at the same time, **both routers will process the message**. There is no automatic mutual exclusion, so the old webhook must be removed as part of the switch. ## Recommended migration approach 1. **Prepare V2 in full.** Recreate your routing setup in V2 (see [Setup comparisons](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/setup-comparisons)). This has no effect on live routing yet. 2. **Cut over one channel at a time.** For each channel, point its inbound webhook at V2 and remove the V1 webhook. Migrating per channel lets you validate each one in isolation and roll back quickly if needed. 3. **Verify, then decommission V1.** Once all channels are routing through V2 and verified, remove the remaining V1 configuration. > 📘 Migration tip > > There is no single global "go live" switch. The per-channel webhook is the cutover control, which is what makes a staged, channel-by-channel migration possible. --- ## Setup comparisons Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/setup-comparisons.md ## Overview Router V1 and Router V2 represent two distinct approaches to configuring and managing routing scenarios. While both versions are designed to facilitate message routing and handovers, they differ fundamentally in their configuration models and operational flexibility. In Router V1, configurations are based on rulesets, which allow you to define all routing scenarios within a single setup. Individual rules pointing to applications can be enabled or disabled dynamically, giving you real-time control over which applications receive messages. This flexibility is further enhanced by the use of a scripted chatbot, which can handle advanced tasks such as initiating handovers or performing routing mutations. In contrast, Router V2 introduces a more structured approach based on flows and states. Rules pointing to applications are always enabled and cannot be toggled on or off. Instead, flexibility is achieved by separating different scenarios into distinct states within a flow. Switching between scenarios is accomplished by activating different states in real time, rather than modifying rules dynamically. This model simplifies configuration management while maintaining the ability to adapt to changing requirements during conversations. ## Scenarios ### Save conversation history #### Router V1 In Router V1, saving conversation history required the use of a Conversation History adapter. This adapter acted as a central repository for storing conversation data. To enable history saving for specific adapters, you would link them to the Conversation History adapter. This setup allowed you to selectively save conversation history for specific interactions, providing granular control over data retention. \[Saving conversation history in Router V1] #### Router V2 In Router V2, the process of saving conversation history has been streamlined. A separate Conversation History connection is no longer required, as conversation history is now saved automatically for all interactions. This eliminates the need for manual configuration and ensures that all conversations are retained by default. To customize the retention period for conversation history, open **Explorer → Settings**. Here, you can specify how many days the history should be retained, allowing you to align data retention policies with your organizational requirements. \[History retention in Explorer → Settings (Router V2)] ### Handover to live agent #### Router V1 In Router V1 all scenarios were configured in one ruleset. By altering rulesets in real-time conversations, you could switch to a different scenario. In example below, an initial ruleset is configured for conversation to happen between Business Messaging and a chatbot. A rule between Business Messaging and Robin (Agent Inbox in Router V2) is disabled. When a bot cannot continue conversation anymore, there will be in real-time rule adjustments to enable rule from Business Messaging to Robin and disable from Business Messaging to bot. This will initiate a scenario handover to a live agent. \[Ruleset for a conversation between bot and channel] #### Router V2 In Router V2, rules cannot be adjusted dynamically during conversations. Instead, you configure states with predefined rules and switch between them in real time. The process begins by setting up a default state, where conversations start. For example, the default state might involve channels communicating with HALO. This state serves as the initial configuration for routing messages. \[Default state configuration] When HALO can no longer handle the conversation and needs to hand over to a live agent, the system switches in real time to another state. In this example, the conversation transitions from HALO to a Live agent state, where channels are configured to communicate with Agent Inbox (Robin in Router V1). This state-based approach ensures smooth transitions between scenarios without requiring manual rule adjustments. \[Handover to live agent state configuration] ### Routing and handing over messages from multiple BM channels #### Router V1 In Router V1, separating Business Messaging (BM) channels along with numbers was technically not possible. However, this limitation was addressed by using the Scripted Chatbot to perform routing mutations or handovers based on specific configurations for channels or channel-and-number combinations. \[Ruleset for routing several BM channels] To separate BM identifiers, you could add a channel or channels with numbers in the **Conversation Owner**. This approach allowed you to create multiple scripts, each with distinct configurations for specific channel identifiers. One method for configuring a bot with specific channel identifiers was to use **Web Requests** blocks to execute routing mutation requests. For example, a routing mutation could disable the rule BM > Bot and enable the rule BM > CAIC WhatsApp. Afterward, the Web Request block could be used again to resend a message to CAIC WhatsApp. This configuration enabled you to add multiple channels, each with distinct routing rules tailored to specific channel identifiers. \[Routing specific channel identifiers using Web Requests block] Another method for configuring a bot with specific channel identifiers - particularly for handing over conversations to live agents - was to use the **Handover** block. This approach allowed you to define different mutation rules and web store referrer values for various channel identifiers, enabling seamless handovers tailored to specific channels. \[Routing specific channel identifiers using Handover block] #### Router V2 In Router V2, the process of routing messages has been significantly streamlined. You can now add channels with specific identifiers and directly link them to different applications, like separate Halo profiles. This enhanced functionality eliminates the need for complex scripted configurations and provides a more intuitive and efficient way to manage routing and handovers. To configure different use cases effectively, it is recommended to create separate flows for each scenario. This approach avoids creating overly complex setups, often referred to as the "wheel of doom/death/hell." By organizing scenarios into distinct flows, you can maintain clarity and simplify management. \[Separate flows for different use cases] The Customer support flow is configured to handle regular conversations between a bot and other channels, with the option to hand over the conversation to a live agent when necessary. This flow includes two states: - **Bot First** state: this state represents the initial configuration where conversations are routed through Conversational AI Cloud. It serves as the starting point for interactions. \[Bot first state] - **Live agent** state: this state is configured to facilitate handovers to live agents. When Conversational AI Cloud can no longer handle the conversation, the system switches to this state, enabling communication between channels and the live agents (Agent Inbox). \[Live agent state] --- ## Onboarding Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/onboarding.md ## Overview The first time you open the Router, the onboarding wizard ("Welcome to the router") helps you configure your account by guiding you through: - **Channels** — select which Business Messaging channels to route through the Router - **HALO** — enable CM.com's agentic AI solution - **Contact center** — connect to Agent Inbox or a Marketplace integration \[Onboarding wizard] ## Prerequisites Before you can proceed with onboarding or configuration, several prerequisites must be fulfilled to ensure the system operates as intended. These requirements apply to channels, HALO profiles, and marketplace integrations. ### Channels Channels must be provisioned in the Channels product to enable onboarding. Without properly configured channels, the onboarding wizard cannot proceed. For more information, refer to the Prerequisites on the [Business Messaging](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/business-messaging) page. If no channels are provisioned for your account, a warning message will appear, providing a link to the Channels management interface. From there, you can provision new channels as needed. ### HALO If you plan to set up HALO, HALO profiles must first be configured within the HALO product itself. If no profiles are available for your account, an informational message will be displayed. In such cases, contact your administrator to request the setup of HALO profiles. ### Marketplace integrations For configuring Marketplace integrations, at least one integration must be provisioned for your account. If no integrations are configured, the Marketplace option will be disabled. ## Configuration ### Channels The Channels section allows you to select which Business Messaging channels should route conversations through the Router. Use the multi-select dropdown to choose one or more channels; each channel displays its sender identifier (e.g., phone number for SMS/WhatsApp, page name for Facebook). Find more information on the [Business Messaging](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/business-messaging) page. ### HALO The HALO section enables CM.com's generative and agentic AI solution. HALO is enabled by default; select which HALO profile you want to use from the dropdown. Find more information on the [HALO](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/halo) page. ### Contact center The Contact center section configures where conversations are routed for agent handling. It is enabled by default; choose between **Agent Inbox** and **Marketplace**. #### Agent Inbox Route conversations directly to CM.com's Agent Inbox solution. To configure it, fill in the appropriate API key. Find more information on the [Agent Inbox](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/agent-inbox) page. > 📘 Advanced settings availability > > Advanced settings are only available to CM employees. #### Marketplace Route conversations to a third-party contact center solution via a Marketplace integration. Select the integration you would like to use from the dropdown. Read more on the [Marketplace](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/marketplace) page. ### Complete onboarding To finalize the onboarding process, click the **Onboard** button. This action automatically creates your channels and applications: if HALO was enabled, a HALO application is created with the selected profile; if Contact center was enabled, an Agent Inbox or Marketplace application is created depending on your choice. Based on the channels and applications chosen during onboarding, a default flow is generated and **published immediately**, so the system is ready to route messages without further manual intervention. The default flow's state is pre-configured with links between your channels and applications. You can review the result on the [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview), [Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications), and [Flows](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows) pages: \[Channels created by onboarding] \[Applications created by onboarding] Based on channels and applications chosen during onboarding, a default flow will be generated and published immediately, ensuring the system is ready to route messages without requiring further manual intervention. \[The generated default flow] The states within the default flow are pre-configured with linked channels and applications, ensuring seamless routing and functionality. This automated setup reduces the need for manual configuration and provides a ready-to-use environment for message routing. \[Generated default states] ### Skip onboarding If you prefer to configure settings manually, click the **Skip** button. If you have entered any data, a confirmation dialog asks whether you want to discard your changes. By skipping onboarding, you retain the flexibility to configure everything manually later — channels, applications, flows, and states can be fully customized through the [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview), [Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications), and [Flows](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows) pages. This option is ideal for users who require a more tailored setup or prefer granular control over the configuration process. --- ## Detection and enrichment steps Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-enrichment-steps.md ## Overview Detection and enrichment steps read a message and add information to it. They never change the text of the message and they never stop it, so they are safe to add to any [pipeline](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines). They run together, after the [guard steps](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards) and before the [transformation steps](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps). What they find is attached to the message that is delivered, shown in the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer), and, where a step has a metadata field, saved on the conversation. ## Language identification **What it does.** Identifies the language of each message, so later steps and your destinations know which language the customer is writing in. **How it works.** Every message is analysed to find the most likely language, out of the 89 [listed below](#recognised-languages). Short messages such as "ok" or a single name are hard to place, so the step does not decide on one message alone. It works with _momentum_: a conversation starts in the default language, and each message adds evidence to the conversation's score. The detected language only switches once the evidence is confident. As a result a one-word reply in another language does not flip a Dutch conversation to English. **Settings.** | Setting | Description | | - | - | | **Default language** | The language a conversation starts in, until detection has enough momentum to switch. Choose from English, Dutch, German, French, Spanish and Italian. Defaults to English. | **What you will see.** The Explorer shows the language detected for each message, for example `Language: Dutch`. The delivered message carries the detected language and how confident the detection was. **Good to know.** - [Translation](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps#translation) in auto-detect mode needs this step. Translation uses the detected language as the language to translate from. - Language identification is free when the pipeline also contains Translation. - The default language is chosen from six languages. Detection itself covers every language in the list below. ### Recognised languages The step recognises these 89 languages: Afrikaans, Albanian, Amharic, Arabic, Armenian, Assamese, Azerbaijani, Basque, Bengali, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Burmese, Catalan, Chinese, Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Filipino, Finnish, French, Galician, Ganda, Georgian, German, Greek, Gujarati, Hebrew, Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Indonesian, Inuktitut, Irish, Italian, Japanese, Javanese, Kannada, Kazakh, Khmer, Korean, Kurdish, Lao, Latvian, Lithuanian, Macedonian, Malay, Malayalam, Maltese, Marathi, Mongolian, Nepali, Norwegian, Odia, Pashto, Persian, Polish, Portuguese, Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Sesotho, Sinhala, Slovak, Slovenian, Somali, Southern Ndebele, Spanish, Sundanese, Swahili, Swati, Swedish, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Tsonga, Tswana, Turkish, Ukrainian, Urdu, Uzbek, Venda, Vietnamese, Welsh, Xhosa and Zulu. Where a language is written in more than one script or variety, it is reported as one language: Serbian in Latin and Cyrillic, Norwegian Bokmål and Nynorsk, the Kurdish varieties, and the Arabic dialects. A language outside this list is not detected, so a message in one is matched to the closest language on the list. ## Named entity extraction **What it does.** Pulls specific details out of a message, such as an order number, a date, or a product, so you can use them without reading the message. **How it works.** You define the entities you want, by name. The step then finds matching values in the message text. There is no list of patterns to maintain: you describe what you are looking for in words, and the step finds it however the customer words it. **Settings.** Add one row for each entity: | Setting | Description | | - | - | | **Entity name** | What to look for, for example `order number`. Select a suggestion or type your own. Suggestions include order number, tracking number, product, brand, size, color, price, payment method, delivery method, store location, date, discount code and return reason. | | **Metadata field** | Optional. The name of a metadata field to store the value in, for example `order_number`. It is filled in automatically from the entity name, and you can change it. | **What you will see.** The Explorer shows how many entities were found, for example `Entities found: 2`. Each entity is attached to the delivered message with its name, the text that was found and how confident the step was. When an entity has a metadata field, the value is saved there. If several values are found they are joined with a comma. **Good to know.** - Choose specific names. `order number` finds more reliable matches than `number`. - The step extracts what is written in the message. It does not look anything up. - Extraction runs before [PII redaction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps#pii-redaction), so it works on the message as the customer wrote it. A detail such as an order number or a name can be captured first, and the message that people read can still be redacted afterwards. For example, a support employee sees `[FULL_NAME_0]` in the message, while the extracted entity or metadata field holds the value your application needs. ## Sentiment analysis **What it does.** Classifies the tone of each message as positive, neutral or negative. **How it works.** The whole message is read and given one label. Sentiment is a judgement about the message as a whole, not about individual products or topics in it. **Settings.** | Setting | Description | | - | - | | **Score context** | Optional. The name of a metadata field to store the sentiment label in, for example `score_context`. | **What you will see.** The Explorer shows the sentiment of each message as Positive, Neutral or Negative. The sentiment is also attached to the delivered message and, when you set a score context, saved in that metadata field. **Good to know.** - Sentiment is scored per message. To follow the mood of a conversation, look at the messages in sequence. ## CXP enrichment **What it does.** Sends the information that this pipeline extracts, the entities and the sentiment, to the CXP. **Why use it.** A message on its own tells an agent little. With this step the CXP receives structured data for every message, next to the conversation itself, so agents and anyone analysing conversations have the context without reading back through the chat: - **Which product a customer is talking about.** An entity such as `product` or `brand` is available as a field, not only as words in a message. - **The right context for an order.** An extracted `order number` is on hand when the conversation reaches an agent, so they can open the order instead of asking for it again. - **How the customer feels.** The sentiment of each message makes frustrated customers easy to spot and to follow over time. **How it works.** The step does not look at the message itself. It switches on the transfer of what Named entity extraction and Sentiment analysis found in the same pipeline. The values are sent for every message as it is processed. **Settings.** None. **Good to know.** - It only has something to send when the pipeline also contains Named entity extraction or Sentiment analysis. - It does not change the message, and it is not billed. --- ## Guard steps Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards.md ## Overview Guard steps protect your destinations, such as agents and bots, from unwanted content. They run first in a [pipeline](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines) and act in one of two ways: - **Filter**: the offending content is masked, neutralised or removed, and the message continues to its destination. - **Quarantine**: the pipeline stops and the message is not delivered. Quarantined messages remain visible in the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer), together with the step that stopped them. Which action a guard takes is fixed for some guards and a setting for others: | Step | Filter | Quarantine | | - | - | - | | [Spam detection](#spam-detection) | No | Always | | [Virus scan](#virus-scan) | Setting | Setting | | [URL reputation](#url-reputation) | Suspected links always; known-malicious links unless set to quarantine | Setting (known-malicious links only) | | [Profanity](#profanity) | Always | No | | [Data loss prevention](#data-loss-prevention) | Always | No | Guards decide on the Router's own confidence in what they find. The thresholds are set by the platform so that ordinary conversations are not interrupted, which is why most guards have few settings. ## Spam detection **What it does.** Quarantines messages that look like spam, so agents never have to see them. **How it works.** The guard looks at how a sender behaves and what they send, judged across the whole conversation rather than one message at a time. For conversations it watches for: - a sender who sends messages unusually fast, - the same content being sent repeatedly, across senders and conversations, - one sender reaching many different conversations in a short time, - a sustained stream of gibberish. For emails it adds checks that apply to mail only: - whether the message really comes from the domain it claims to come from, using cryptographic validation of the sender, - whether the reply address, display name, or sender domain imitates a different organisation, including your own, - whether links show one address but lead somewhere else, - whether the email hides text from the reader, - an analysis of the content itself. No single weak sign quarantines a message. The signals are combined into one confidence, and the message is only quarantined when that confidence is high. A legitimate customer writing from a shared mailbox or forwarding a shipping notice should not be caught. **Settings.** None. Which signals count and how strongly is managed by the platform. **What you will see.** A quarantined message is not delivered. The Explorer marks the destination and the Spam guard step as **Blocked** and lists the signals that contributed. When nothing was quarantined it shows what was observed instead, or _None_. **Good to know.** - Only messages sent by your customers are judged, not replies from your agents or bots. - Because the judgement covers the conversation, a sender who has been sending junk is more likely to be quarantined than a first-time sender with a single odd message. ## Virus scan **What it does.** Scans attachments for malware before they reach an agent or application. **How it works.** Every attachment on the message, for example an image, document or archive, is scanned with an antivirus engine. The engine looks inside archives as well. Files that have been scanned before are recognised, so the same file is not scanned again. **Settings.** Under _When an attachment is infected_, choose what happens to an infected attachment: | Action | Result | | - | - | | **Filter the attachment** | The infected attachment is removed and the message continues. For a media message that carries only the attachment, the message is removed. For an email, only that attachment is removed and the body is still delivered. | | **Quarantine** | The message is not delivered. | **What you will see.** The Explorer shows _Clean_, _Infected_ with the name of the threat, or _Skipped (no attachment)_. A quarantined message is marked **Blocked**. **Good to know.** - Attachments over 100 MB cannot be scanned. They are always removed, whichever action you selected, but the rest of the message is still delivered. - A file that cannot be retrieved for scanning is never delivered. - Virus scan is billed per attachment scanned rather than per message. It runs after Spam detection, so a message that spam detection quarantines is never scanned or billed. ## URL reputation **What it does.** Protects agents and customers from phishing and malware links in message text. **How it works.** 1. The guard finds every link in the message, including links written in an obscured form such as `hxxp://` or with `[.]` instead of dots. 2. It follows each link through any redirects to find where it really leads. 3. It checks that destination against lists of known phishing and malware addresses and against signs of a suspicious link, such as characteristics of the address itself and how recently the domain was registered. 4. Each link gets one of two verdicts: | Verdict | Meaning | What happens | | - | - | - | | **Suspected** | The link shows signs of being malicious. | The link is always neutralised. It can never quarantine the message. | | **Known malicious** | The destination appears on a list of known malicious addresses. | The link is neutralised, or the message is quarantined, depending on your setting. | Neutralising a link, also called defanging, keeps it readable but stops it being clickable. `https://example.com/login` becomes `hxxps://example[.]com/login`. The reader can still see what was in the message. **Settings.** Under _When a risky link is found_, choose what happens to a known-malicious link: | Action | Result | | - | - | | **Filter suspected links** | All risky links, suspected and known-malicious, are neutralised and the message continues. | | **Quarantine known, filter suspicious** | A message containing a known-malicious link is not delivered. Suspected links are neutralised and the message continues. | **What you will see.** The delivered text shows the neutralised links. The Explorer shows _No URLs found_, or whether the links were checked or flagged. A quarantined message is marked **Blocked**. **Good to know.** - A link is judged by where it really leads, so a shortened or redirected link is checked on its final destination. ## Profanity **What it does.** Masks abusive and harmful language, so agents and downstream applications do not receive it. **How it works.** The message is analysed by a multilingual language model that finds harmful passages and the category they belong to. Passages in the categories you selected are replaced with asterisks and the rest of the message is delivered as is. **Settings.** Select the categories to look for. At least one must be selected before the step can be saved. | Category | Covers | | - | - | | **Profanity** | Swearing and vulgar language. | | **Sexual content** | Sexually explicit language. | | **Hate speech** | Language that attacks people for who they are. | | **Violence** | Threats and descriptions of violence. | | **Self-harm** | Language about harming oneself. | **What you will see.** The delivered message contains asterisks in place of the masked passages. The Explorer shows how many passages were masked, or _None_. **Good to know.** - The guard only masks. Quarantining is not available for this step. - It works across languages, not only English. ## Data loss prevention **What it does.** Masks secrets and credentials that someone pastes into a conversation, so they are not passed on to agents, bots or other applications. **How it works.** The message text is scanned for patterns that look like secrets and the matching values are replaced with a label naming what was found, for example `[REDACTED:Tokens]`. For an assignment such as a password or a connection string only the value is masked, so the message stays readable. Examples and placeholder values, such as `password=changeme`, are recognised and left alone so that ordinary text is not masked. The guard detects: - JWT tokens, - common API keys, - encryption keys, such as private keys, - cloud credentials, - connection strings, - passwords (best effort). This is different from [PII redaction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps#pii-redaction), which masks personal details such as names and phone numbers. The two can be used together. **Settings.** None. The guard always scans for all of the secret types above. Password detection is best effort, because a password has no fixed shape. **What you will see.** The delivered message contains the labelled mask. The Explorer shows what kinds of secrets were masked, for example `1 token`, but never the secrets themselves. **Good to know.** - The guard only masks. It does not quarantine messages. - It runs before the analysis steps, so Named entity extraction, Sentiment analysis and Translation never see the secret. --- ## Pipelines Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines.md ## Overview A pipeline is a set of processing steps applied to messages as they travel over a route within a state. Pipelines let the Router protect and prepare traffic on its way to a destination: - **Protect** your agents and applications from spam, malware, malicious links, abusive language, and leaked credentials. - **Understand** each message by detecting its language, extracting the details you care about, and scoring its sentiment. - **Transform** the message before delivery by redacting personal data or translating it into the language your team works in. Pipelines are managed on the **Pipelines** page and attached to individual routes in the flow editor, so different routes can process messages differently. For example, you can translate only what goes to your agents, and redact personal data only on the route to an external AI service. \[Pipelines overview] ## The steps at a glance | Step | Type | What it does | Settings | | - | - | - | - | | [Spam detection](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards#spam-detection) | Guard | Quarantines spam, judged over the whole conversation. | None | | [Virus scan](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards#virus-scan) | Guard | Scans attachments for malware. | Remove the attachment or quarantine the message | | [URL reputation](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards#url-reputation) | Guard | Neutralises suspicious and known-malicious links. | Whether known-malicious links quarantine the message | | [Profanity](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards#profanity) | Guard | Masks abusive and harmful language. | Categories to look for | | [Data loss prevention](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards#data-loss-prevention) | Guard | Masks secrets and credentials. | None | | [Language identification](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-enrichment-steps#language-identification) | Enrichment | Detects the language of each message. | Default language | | [Named entity extraction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-enrichment-steps#named-entity-extraction) | Enrichment | Pulls out the details you define, such as order numbers. | Entities to extract, and the metadata field for each | | [Sentiment analysis](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-enrichment-steps#sentiment-analysis) | Enrichment | Classifies the tone of each message. | Optional metadata field name | | [CXP enrichment](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-enrichment-steps#cxp-enrichment) | Enrichment | Sends the extracted entities and sentiment to the CXP. | None | | [PII redaction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps#pii-redaction) | Transformation | Replaces personal data with placeholders. | Types of personal data to redact | | [Translation](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps#translation) | Transformation | Translates messages between your customers' language and yours. | Customer language and your team's language | ## How a pipeline runs ### Fixed order The order in which steps run is decided by the Router, not by the order you add them in. Steps are grouped into stages. Stages run one after another, and the steps inside a stage run at the same time. | Stage | Steps | Why here | | - | - | - | | 1 | Spam detection, Profanity | These guards judge the message as it was written, so they run first and spam detection can stop it before anything else happens. | | 2 | URL reputation, Virus scan | The two guards that take the most work, following links and scanning attachments, run only on messages that spam detection let through. URL reputation rewrites links, and Virus scan looks at attachments instead of text. | | 3 | Data loss prevention | Masks secrets before any later step sees the text. | | 4 | Language identification, Named entity extraction, Sentiment analysis, CXP enrichment | Read the message and add information to it without changing it. | | 5 | PII redaction | Rewrites the message. | | 6 | Translation | Rewrites the message. Runs last so the delivered text is in the language your team reads. | Two consequences are worth knowing: - Steps that analyse the message (stage 4) see the text after links have been neutralised and secrets masked, but before personal data is redacted and before translation. - Redaction runs before translation, so translation only ever sees the placeholders, never the personal data itself. ### Quarantine stops the pipeline When a guard quarantines a message, the pipeline stops immediately: no later step runs and the message is not delivered to the destination. The message and the reason it was quarantined stay visible in the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer). ### One of each step Each step type can be added to a pipeline once. A pipeline that uses translation in auto-detect mode must also include Language identification, because translation needs to know which language the customer wrote in. If you pin the customer's language in the translation step, Language identification is not needed. ### Which messages are processed - Pipelines process messages that travel over the route. Conversation events, such as the start or end of a session, are passed along untouched. - Steps look at text. For emails, the whole body is processed, including tables and signatures. - Virus scan looks at attachments instead of text. - Spam detection judges messages sent by your customers only. - Translation works in both directions: customer messages are translated to your team's language, and replies are translated back into the customer's language. ### Delivery comes first A pipeline should never be the reason a conversation stalls. If the pipeline as a whole cannot complete, for example because a processing service is temporarily unavailable, the message is still delivered, without the processing that could not run. The problem is recorded with the run, and you can see which steps ran in the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer). The exception is content that cannot be vouched for: an attachment that could not be scanned is not delivered. ### Channels that stream messages Some channels deliver messages in live parts as they are being written, for example Web Conversations with an AI agent. When a route's pipeline can change or withhold a message (every step except Language identification, Named entity extraction, Sentiment analysis and CXP enrichment), the live parts are held back and the recipient receives the finished, processed message instead. This guarantees nobody sees text that a step would have changed or blocked. ## Managing pipelines - **Add pipeline** creates a new pipeline and opens the editor. - Click a pipeline, or choose **Edit** in its Actions menu, to edit it. The Actions menu also offers **Delete**. ## Editing a pipeline The editor shows the pipeline's steps as a timeline, in the order they run. Steps are placed in their stage automatically, so a step you add later can appear above earlier ones. Select a step to see and change its settings in a tab in the panel on the right. Click **Save** to save the pipeline. \[Pipeline editor with a guard step selected] Click **Add step** to add a step type: \[Add step dialog] Steps that need another step show which one. Steps you have already added are not offered again. The **Pricing details** tab in the panel on the right shows what the pipeline costs. See [Billing](#billing). ## Applying a pipeline A pipeline is attached to a **route** inside a state. In the flow editor each state is a table, and each row is a route with a source, a direction (**One way**, **Both ways** or **Stop**) and a destination: 1. Open the flow on the **Flows** page. Each state is shown as its own table of routes. 2. In the row of the route you want, click the cog wheel at the end of the row. A tab for that route opens in the panel on the right. 3. Under **Pipeline**, select the pipeline to apply from the dropdown. Select **None** to remove it. 4. Click **Save** to save the flow. The cog wheel is shown once both ends of the route are set. Routes that carry calls have no cog wheel, because pipelines only process messages. A route that goes both ways shows one dropdown per direction, so you can apply a different pipeline to each direction, or to only one of them. Once a pipeline is selected, the panel shows its steps and a button to open it. Messages travelling over that route, and only that route, are processed by the pipeline. One pipeline can be attached to as many routes as you like, and each direction of a route can only have one pipeline. A pipeline on one direction does not process traffic on the other. When you open a pipeline on the **Pipelines** page, **Where this pipeline runs** lists the flows and routes it is attached to. ## Reading the results Each step leaves a trace you can use. ### In the Explorer Open a conversation in the [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer) and expand the routing detail of a message. For every destination it shows: - the text that was actually delivered, next to the original, - each step that ran and what it found, such as the detected language, the entities extracted, or what a guard acted on, - whether a guard quarantined the message. The routing detail is headed by the flow and state, and says _Routed to 1 destination_ or _Routed to N destinations_. Each destination shows its delivered text, a **Blocked** tag when a guard quarantined the message, and a **Pipeline** list with one line per step that ran. A step that could not complete is marked **Failed**. The line of each step says what it found: | Step | What the Explorer shows | | - | - | | Spam guard | The signals behind a quarantine, or, when nothing was quarantined, the observations and scores recorded, or _None_. | | Antivirus guard | _Clean_, _Infected_ with the threat names, _Skipped (no attachment)_, or _Anti-Virus unexpected error_. | | Url guard | _No URLs found_, or whether links were checked or flagged. | | Profanity guard | The number of masked passages, or _None_. | | Data loss prevention guard | The kinds of secrets masked, or _None_. | | Language identification | `Language: Dutch`. | | Named entity extraction | `Entities found: 2`. | | Sentiment analysis | Positive, Neutral or Negative. | | PII redaction | `Redacted: 2 phone numbers, 1 name`, or _Nothing detected_. | | Translation | `Translated Dutch -> English`, or _No translation needed_. | Besides the Explorer, the History API reports an outcome for every delivery: `delivered`, `translated`, `redacted`, `filtered` or `blocked`. When more than one applies, the most severe wins, in that order from `blocked` down to `translated`. ### On the delivered message Steps that detect something attach their findings to the message that is delivered, so the destination can use them: the detected language, the entities extracted, the sentiment, the redactions with their original values, and, for translated messages, the original text. ### As conversation metadata Named entity extraction and Sentiment analysis can store what they found in a metadata field that you name. The values are saved on the conversation, so they are available beyond the single message. ## Example pipelines **Agents who speak one language, customers who speak many.** Add Language identification and Translation. Customer messages arrive in your team's language, and agent replies reach each customer in theirs. **Safe inbox for an email channel.** Add Spam detection, Virus scan and URL reputation. Spam is quarantined, infected attachments are removed, and links that look malicious are made unclickable before an agent sees them. **Sending to an external AI service.** Add Data loss prevention and PII redaction on the route to the AI service, so credentials and personal data are masked in the message text before it is delivered. Keep in mind that the original personal values still travel with the message as enrichment (see [PII redaction](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps#pii-redaction)), so use this setup for services that read the message text. **Routing on what the customer wrote.** Add Named entity extraction for an order number and Sentiment analysis, and store both in metadata fields to use them downstream. ## Billing Steps are billed per thousand units, and only when they are executed. Most steps are billed per message; Virus scan is billed per attachment scanned. A step that does not run is not billed: once a guard quarantines a message, the steps in later stages are not executed or billed. For example, when Spam detection quarantines an email, its attachments are not scanned and no Virus scan is billed. Language identification is free when the same pipeline also contains Translation. The editor shows the price of each step under **Pricing details**. ## Next steps - [Guard steps](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards): spam, virus, URL, profanity and data loss prevention. - [Detection and enrichment steps](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-enrichment-steps): language, entities, sentiment and CXP. - [Transformation steps](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps): PII redaction and translation. --- ## Transformation steps Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-transformation-steps.md ## Overview Transformation steps change the text of a message before it is delivered. They run last in a [pipeline](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines), PII redaction first and Translation after it, so the message that arrives is the finished result of every earlier step. Both steps keep what they changed: PII redaction keeps the original values and Translation keeps the original text. Both travel with the delivered message as enrichment, so a destination that is allowed to see them can use them. ## PII redaction **What it does.** Replaces personal details in a message with placeholders, so the destination receives the message without them. **How it works.** The step finds personal identifiers in the text, across languages, and replaces each one with a numbered placeholder that says what kind of detail was removed, for example `[FULL_NAME_0]`. The same value always gets the same placeholder within a message, so a name mentioned three times stays one person, and two different names stay two. The message is still readable and meaning is preserved. > Original: `Hi, I am Jan de Vries, call me on 06 12345678.` > Delivered: `Hi, I am [FULL_NAME_0], call me on [PHONE_NUMBER_0].` **Settings.** Select the personal identifiers to redact: | Identifier | Examples | | - | - | | **Full name** | A person's first and last name. | | **Phone number** | A mobile or landline number. | | **Email address** | An email address. | | **Postal address** | A street address. | | **Payment card number** | A credit or debit card number. | | **Bank account number** | An IBAN or other account number. | **What you will see.** The delivered message contains the placeholders. The Explorer shows a _Redacted_ line on the PII redaction step that counts what was replaced by kind, for example `Redacted: 2 phone numbers, 1 name`, or _Nothing detected_. It names the kinds, never the values. **The original values.** The text of the message is redacted, but the original values are not thrown away. Each redaction is attached to the delivered message as enrichment, with its label, the original value and the placeholder that replaced it. This lets an application that is allowed to handle personal data, such as the one that completes an order, map a placeholder back to the person. Anyone who reads only the message text, such as a support employee in an inbox, sees only the placeholders. **Good to know.** - Because the enrichment carries the original values, treat it as personal data. The transcription endpoint of the History API leaves enrichment out unless you ask for it with `includeEnrichment=true`. The pipeline's own record of the run, which is kept in the conversation history, holds the labels and placeholders but not the original values. - Only the types you select are redacted. Anything else in the message is delivered as written. - Detection is based on context, so it can find names and addresses that follow no fixed pattern. As with any automatic detection, it can miss some values and occasionally mark text that is not personal. - To mask credentials and secrets rather than personal details, use [Data loss prevention](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipeline-guards#data-loss-prevention). - Redaction is applied before Translation, so a translation never contains the personal data either. ## Translation **What it does.** Lets customers and your team each use their own language. Customer messages are translated into your team's language, and replies are translated back. **How it works.** The step translates in both directions: - Messages from the customer are translated from the customer's language into the **host language**, the language your team or application works in. - Messages from your side, which are assumed to be written in the host language, are translated into the customer's language. The customer's language is found in one of two ways: - **Auto detect.** The language of each conversation is detected by the Language identification step, which this mode requires. Replies go out in the language the customer has been writing in. - **A fixed language.** You choose the customer language yourself. Language identification is not needed, and every customer message is treated as written in that language. A message that is already in the target language is passed through unchanged. So is a message without any words to translate, such as `???` or a number. **Settings.** | Setting | Description | | - | - | | **Client language** | The language your customers write in: **Auto detect**, or one of English, Dutch, German, French, Spanish and Italian. | | **Host language** | The language your team or application works in. Choose from English, Dutch, German, French, Spanish and Italian. | For advanced cases, such as an agent who reads a different language per conversation, the host language can also be set through the APIs. **What you will see.** The delivered message is the translation, and the original text is attached to it as enrichment. In the Explorer the Translation step shows the languages involved, for example `Translated Dutch -> English`, or _No translation needed_ when the message was already in the target language. **Good to know.** - Values that earlier steps have put in place are kept as they are: redaction placeholders, masked secrets, neutralised links and extracted entity values are not translated. If one of them cannot be kept intact, the message is delivered untranslated rather than with a gap in it. - Emails are translated block by block. An email is billed as one translation however many blocks it has. - Translation is automatic. Names, product terms and very short messages can come out differently than a human translator would choose. - Language identification is free when the pipeline also contains Translation. --- ## Introduction Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/router-introduction.md The Router is CM.com's central message-routing platform for all chat applications. It forwards incoming messages to designated target applications and enables two-way communication between all connected applications. We currently support two versions: - **Version 1 (V1)**: the legacy release in maintenance mode. - **Version 2 (V2)**: the actively supported and continuously developed release. The Conversational Router routes messages based on a configuration that you define. To make setup as clear and simple as possible, we provide a visual configuration builder for creating and maintaining this configuration. A configuration in the Conversational Router consists of: - **flows**: a use case or scenario. Example: "Help the customer with a bot; if that doesn't succeed, hand over to a human agent." - **states**: the routing behavior at a specific point within a flow (i.e., where messages are routed at that moment). In the example above, the first state routes the customer to a bot; the second state routes the customer to an agent. If you would like to know more about states and how to switch between them, please see [States](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states). Below is an implementation of the first state — the customer talks to a bot over the grouped WhatsApp and SMS channels, configured visually in the flow editor: \[A state in the flow editor] In the state shown above, links define the message flow in both directions between the support channels and the bot. When the bot determines it can no longer assist the customer, it initiates a handover to a live agent by activating the second state, in which messages flow bidirectionally between the channels and Agent Inbox instead. ### The Router at a glance Inside the Router you will find: - [Home](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/home) — a dashboard of your routed traffic. - [Channels](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/channels-overview) — the messaging channels your customers reach you on, optionally organized in groups. - [Applications](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/applications) — the destinations conversations are routed to (bots, agent inboxes, integrations). - [Flows](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows) and [States](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states) — the visual routing configuration. - [Pipelines](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines) — per-link message processing such as translation and content guards. - [Explorer](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/explorer) — browse and inspect routed conversations. The platform's APIs are exposed externally, so third parties can integrate their own systems and benefit from the existing ecosystem of applications already connected to the Router. To explore what's possible, browse our ready-made [Connections](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/connections) or learn how to build a [Custom integration](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/custom-integration) to connect your own service. --- ## States Source: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/states.md ## Overview A state is a distinct phase within a flow that determines how messages are routed at a given moment. Each state specifies which connections participate (for example, Conversational AI Cloud and a WhatsApp channel) and the directional links that define who sends messages to whom. One state is marked as the default and is used at the start of a new conversation; you can switch the active state in real time via our [Routing control API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/routing-control-api) to adapt the conversation (for example, hand over from bot to live agent). Think of a flow as the use case ("help the customer with a bot; if that doesn't succeed, hand over to a human agent") and of its states as the phases of that use case: the first state routes the customer to the bot, the second routes the customer to the agent. ## Where states live in the app States are configured inside the flow editor: open the **Flows** page, select a flow, and find the **States** card. Each state is a tab above the canvas; the selected state's routing is drawn as a graph of the flow's connected channels and applications. \[States inside the flow editor] > 📘 State reusability > > A state name is defined once per account and can be reused across flows. For example, with a flow per channel you can use the same "Contact Center" state in all of them. Each flow then holds its own link configuration for that state. ## Configuration ### Add a state In the flow editor's States card, click **Add state**. The dialog offers two tabs: - **Use existing** — pick a state name already defined on your account (for example one used in another flow). - **Create new** — type a name to define a new state. \[Add state dialog] The first state you add to a flow automatically becomes its default state. ### Define the routing links Select the state's tab to see the graph. The nodes are the channels, channel groups, and applications connected to the flow; links between them define the routing. To create a link, drag a connection from the source node to the target node. Each link is a one-way path, so for a two-way conversation you create links in both directions. States allow flexible routing configurations, such as fanning out from one connection to multiple targets — for example, route SMS messages to your bot while simultaneously mirroring them to a custom integration. If a connection you expect to use isn't visible in the graph, return to the flow's **Channels** / **Applications** sections to connect it first (see [Flows](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/flows)). Selecting a link opens a panel where you can delete the link or attach a **pipeline** to it — a sequence of processing steps (translation, content guards, and more) applied to messages travelling over that link. See [Pipelines](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/pipelines). ### Default state If a state is intended to be the starting point for conversations in the flow, click the star icon above the graph to designate it as the default state. The default state determines where new conversations begin. > 📘 Default state > > Only one default state is allowed per flow. Existing conversations remain in their current state unless explicitly switched. To change the active state of a running conversation, use the [Routing control API](https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/guides/routing-control-api). ### Delete a state configuration To remove a state from the flow, select its tab and click the trashcan icon above the graph. > ❗️ Deleting a state configuration > > Deletion is permanent once you save the flow. The default state of a published flow cannot be deleted — first designate another state as the default, or unpublish the flow. --- ## Conversational Router API endpoints (v1) API reference: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/v1/api-reference Base URL: `https://core-node-h3cjyx4jzq-ez.a.run.app` ### POST /public/connect/{configurationId}/adapters/{adapterId}/custom Call any endpoint on the CM.com adapter for the specified configuration Call any endpoint on the specified Connect adapter --- ## Conversational Router API endpoints (v2) API reference: https://docs.cm.com/conversational-router/v2/api-reference Base URL: `https://core-node-h3cjyx4jzq-ez.a.run.app` ### POST /public/connect/{configurationId}/adapters/{adapterId}/custom Call any endpoint on the CM.com adapter for the specified configuration Call any endpoint on the specified Connect adapter --- # Customer Engagement > Manage customer service inboxes, run marketing campaigns, track behavior, and automate outreach. --- ## Agent Inbox Source: https://docs.cm.com/customer-engagement/agent-inbox.md Integrate with the Agent Inbox helpdesk platform.
